title: Using Finale and not trusting playback
summary: He uses Finale for extracting parts but writes faster by hand, and told students not to trust playback.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. It’s a unique sound for that time. You must have transitioned, well I should say and ask, do you now use software, Finale or Sibelius or whatever?

Yeah I use Finale only because I can extract the parts. I hate copying parts. I can write faster with a score pad and pencil. I think Gordon Goodwin can as well and Mark Taylor as well. But after you’ve got the sketch done, for me now once I’ve got it in my head I just put it down in the computer and then you can extract the parts. Because that’s the hardest part is writing out the parts.
That’s for sure. But can you tell if using Finale has changed the way you write?

No it hasn’t. As a matter of fact when I was teaching, I just retired a few years ago, I would make it a point to all my students that you cannot use the playback of Finale or Sibelius or any of those. Do not listen to the playback. If you listen to a playback make everything piano. Because you’re going to get fooled because the instrument has no overtones. I’ve put in, just as an example for the kids, I’ve put in Thad Jones’s “Quietitude” I put that in Finale, I put in Gil Evans’s “My Ship,” I put that in Finale. And I’ve got the best sound libraries you can buy. All right? And I play it back to the kids. It sounds like crap. You wouldn’t dare write that, because that doesn’t sound right. And they hear the sounds, “Oh that’s not right” so they take it away. They’re afraid to put the sharp nine and the natural nine together, you know, in a dominant seven chord because the machine doesn’t like it you know. It sounds awful. So they won’t take a chance. And that’s the one thing I really pounded into their heads that you cannot do that. And no it doesn’t affect me but it might affect younger writers today. They might, you know, take the easy way out because the machine tells them that, or the sounds.
